summary.text: A finite evaluation of the recurrence through index 20 shows that \(13^2\mid a(20)\). Since 13 is coprime to both 2 and 3, any factorization \(a(20)=2^r3^s m\) would force \(13^2\mid m\), contradicting that \(m\) is squarefree.

full_proof.text:
Let \(d(x)\) denote the number of decimal digits of a nonnegative integer \(x\), with the convention \(d(0)=1\). Thus
\[
C(x,y)=x10^{d(y)}+y
\]
is the decimal concatenation of \(x\) followed by \(y\). Define the sequence by
\[
a(1)=0,\qquad a(2)=1,
\]
and, for \(n\geq 3\),
\[
a(n)=\left|C(a(n-1),a(n-2))-C(a(n-2),a(n-1))\right|.
\]
We will show that the conjectured squarefree representation fails at \(n=20\).

For brevity, put
\[
\ell_n=d(a(n)),\qquad q_n\equiv 10^{\ell_n}\pmod {169},
\qquad r_n\equiv a(n)\pmod {169},
\]
where the displayed representatives for \(q_n\) and \(r_n\) below lie between \(0\) and \(168\). Also define the signed, pre-absolute-value difference
\[
D_n=C(a(n-1),a(n-2))-C(a(n-2),a(n-1)).
\]
Expanding the two concatenations gives the useful identity
\[
D_n=a(n-1)(10^{\ell_{n-2}}-1)
     -a(n-2)(10^{\ell_{n-1}}-1).                 \tag{1}
\]
If \(\sigma_n=+\) when \(D_n\geq0\), and \(\sigma_n=-\) when \(D_n<0\), then \(a(n)=D_n\) in the first case and \(a(n)=-D_n\) in the second. Consequently, modulo 169,
\[
D_n\equiv r_{n-1}(q_{n-2}-1)-r_{n-2}(q_{n-1}-1),                 \tag{2}
\]
and \(r_n\) is this residue or its negative according as \(\sigma_n\) is \(+\) or \(-\).

The following finite calculation applies (1) successively. The column headed \(t_n\) is the least nonnegative residue of \(D_n\) modulo 169, before taking the absolute value. The sign column records the sign of the actual integer \(D_n\), not merely the sign of a residue.

\[
\begin{array}{c|r|c|r|r|r}
n&\ell_n&\sigma_n&q_n=10^{\ell_n}\bmod169&r_n=a(n)\bmod169&t_n=D_n\bmod169\\ \hline
1&1& &10&0& \\
2&1& &10&1& \\
3&1&+&10&9&9\\
4&2&+&100&72&72\\
5&3&-&155&74&95\\
6&5&-&121&44&125\\
7&8&+&165&93&93\\
8&13&-&23&112&57\\
9&19&+&114&98&98\\
10&32&+&87&147&147\\
11&51&-&116&98&71\\
12&83&-&121&27&142\\
13&133&+&153&133&133\\
14&216&+&92&26&26\\
15&349&-&49&39&130\\
16&565&-&114&65&104\\
17&913&-&153&104&65\\
18&1478&+&35&13&13\\
19&2391&-&116&39&130\\
20&3869&-&4&0&0
\end{array}
\]

Here is a detailed explanation of this finite calculation. Beginning with \(a(1)=0\) and \(a(2)=1\), direct decimal concatenation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=9,\\
a(4)&=72,\\
a(5)&=243,\\
a(6)&=47871,\\
a(7)&=23523372,\\
a(8)&=2434786275501,\\
a(9)&=8244905115337247871,\\
a(10)&=58101188398354233807319449027630,\\
a(11)&=243478627550182449084906698122045988902204111779759,\\
a(12)&=33753325643335988898828779215425644588407139004473126805509723691755094884662752129.
\end{aligned}
\]
These values already exhibit the first twelve digit lengths in the table. Continuing the same integer calculation through \(n=20\) gives digit lengths
\[
133,216,349,565,913,1478,2391,3869
\]
for indices \(13,14,\ldots,20\), respectively, and gives the signs shown in the table. Concretely, at each stage one computes the integer on the right side of (1), compares it with zero to obtain \(\sigma_n\), and checks
\[
10^{\ell_n-1}\leq |D_n|<10^{\ell_n}
\]
to obtain its decimal length. Thus the length and sign columns do not make any assumption about modular representatives; they come from ordinary integer comparisons. Notice that the listed lengths follow the Fibonacci-type pattern \(\ell_n=\ell_{n-1}+\ell_{n-2}\) from \(n=4\) onward, but only the finitely many displayed instances are needed here.

Once the lengths and signs are known, all remaining columns involve only arithmetic modulo 169. The \(q_n\) column is obtained by repeated modular exponentiation of 10 to the listed lengths. Formula (2) then gives \(t_n\), and
\[
r_n=\begin{cases}
t_n,&\sigma_n=+,\\
169-t_n,&\sigma_n=-\text{ and }t_n\ne0,\\
0,&t_n=0.
\end{cases}
\]
For example, at \(n=5\), the preceding data are
\[
r_4=72,\quad r_3=9,\quad q_3=10,\quad q_4=100.
\]
Therefore
\[
D_5\equiv72(10-1)-9(100-1)=648-891=-243\equiv95\pmod{169}.
\]
The actual difference is negative, so \(a(5)=-D_5\), and hence
\[
r_5\equiv-95\equiv74\pmod{169},
\]
as recorded.

Most importantly, the final step can be seen directly from the last preceding two rows. At indices 18 and 19 we have
\[
r_{18}=13,\qquad r_{19}=39,
\]
and
\[
q_{18}=35,\qquad q_{19}=116.
\]
Thus (2) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{20}
&\equiv r_{19}(q_{18}-1)-r_{18}(q_{19}-1)\pmod{169}\\
&\equiv39(35-1)-13(116-1)\pmod{169}\\
&=39\cdot34-13\cdot115\\
&=1326-1495\\
&=-169\equiv0\pmod{169}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking an absolute value does not change divisibility, so
\[
169=13^2\mid a(20).                                      \tag{3}
\]

We now show that (3) is incompatible with the proposed form. Suppose, for contradiction, that the conjecture were true. Since \(20>2\), its squarefree-factor assertion at \(n=20\) would provide nonnegative integers \(r,s\) and a squarefree nonnegative integer \(m\) such that
\[
a(20)=2^r3^s m.                                         \tag{4}
\]
(The conjecture also asserts divisibility by 3, but that other conjunct is irrelevant to the contradiction.)

The number 169 is coprime to both 2 and 3, and therefore it is coprime to \(2^r3^s\). Combining (3) and (4), we have
\[
169\mid 2^r3^s m.
\]
Euclid's coprime cancellation principle says that if \(u\mid vw\) and \(\gcd(u,v)=1\), then \(u\mid w\). Applying it with
\[
u=169,
\qquad v=2^r3^s,
\qquad w=m
\]
yields
\[
169\mid m,
\]
or equivalently
\[
13^2\mid m.                                             \tag{5}
\]

By definition, an integer is squarefree precisely when it is not divisible by the square of any nonunit integer (equivalently, no prime square divides it). But 13 is not a unit among the nonnegative integers, and (5) says that its square divides \(m\). Hence \(m\) is not squarefree, contradicting the requirement in (4).

Thus no representation \(a(20)=2^r3^s m\) with \(m\) squarefree exists. Since \(20>2\), this single term is a counterexample to the universal conjecture. Therefore the stated conjecture about A070823 is false.
